body:
Recently  I encountered the same problem - the worker's memory was not released upon an exception. A fairly large amount of data was generated in the task - about a hundred megabytes, then an error occurred. Each time an error occurred, the worker's resident memory increased by one hundred megabytes and was not released. Worker memory usage was limited to four gigabytes, and by running tasks it was possible to reach this value, after which the worker crashed.

After some investigating, I found that the answer indeed lies in traceback. From the [python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/compound_stmts.html#:~:text=Exceptions%20are%20cleared%20because%20with%20the%20traceback%20attached%20to%20them%2C%20they%20form%20a%20reference%20cycle%20with%20the%20stack%20frame%2C%20keeping%20all%20locals%20in%20that%20frame%20alive%20until%20the%20next%20garbage%20collection%20occurs.):

> Exceptions are cleared because with the traceback attached to them, they form a reference cycle with the stack frame, keeping all locals in that frame alive until the next garbage collection occurs.

Celery creates variables with an exception object, which creates a reference cycle, but actually it takes this into account and cleans up the traceback: 

https://github.com/celery/celery/blob/d1c35bbdf014f13f4ab698d75e3ea381a017b090/celery/app/trace.py#L272-L291

However, the point seems to be that it doesn't take into account that exceptions can be nested.


Let's imagine the following situation:

```
def foo():
    foo_data = ... # there are some local data
    raise SomeException()


@app.task
def actual_task():
    task_data = ... # there are some local data
    try:
        foo()
    except Exception:
        raise SomeAnotherException()

```
So `clear_traceback` function will clear `task_data`, but not `foo_data`.
To clear `foo_data`, `clear_traceback` must not only clear `exc.__traceback__`, but also `exc.__context__.__traceback__` if `__context__` is not `None`. Exception in `__context__` might have its own `__context__`, so is seems that clearing must be done recursively, something like this in the end of  `traceback_clear`:

```
if exc.__context__ is not None:
    traceback_clear(exc.__context__)
```

In the example of ralphie0112358 there are not any nested exceptions, and I could not reproduced the issue with it. But when I added a nested exception with the generation of a large amount of data, the situation with unreleased memory was consistently reproduced.
Perhaps the increase in memory in ralphie0112358 example was not related to the problem I described, but the increase in memory in production was.

Is seems that for now the solution is indeed to call `gc.collect()` directly or not to use nested exceptions.

Anyway, hopefully this will be fixed in future versions.

## Minimally Reproducible Test Case

```python import datetime import logging import random import time from celery import Celery, group from celery.utils.log import get_task_logger from pydantic import BaseModel logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO) logger = get_task_logger(__name__) app = Celery( "celery_mem_leak_test", broker="redis://localhost:6379/0", backend="redis://localhost:6379/0", result_expires=datetime.timedelta(seconds=60), task_serializer="json", ) class DataPoint(BaseModel): time: int value: float class DataProcessorResult(BaseModel): data: list[DataPoint] @app.task(acks_late=True, pydantic=True) def first_stage(message: bytes) -> DataProcessorResult: lines = message.decode("utf-8").splitlines() data = [] for line in lines: timestamp, value = line.split(",") data.append(DataPoint(time=int(timestamp), value=float(value))) return DataProcessorResult(data=data) @app.task(acks_late=True, pydantic=True) def group_task(result: DataProcessorResult): logger.info(f"Got {len(result.data)} data points") @app.task(ignore_result=True) def last_stage(): logger.info("Finished task") NUM_POINTS = 100 NUM_DISTINCT_PAYLOADS = 10 PACKET_DELAY = 1 NUM_GROUP_TASKS = 5 def main(): # Initialize payloads payloads = [] for i in range(NUM_DISTINCT_PAYLOADS): data = [(random.randint(0, 1000), random.random()) for _ in range(NUM_POINTS)] payload = "\n".join(f"{d[0]},{d[1]}" for d in data) payloads.append(payload.encode("utf-8")) while True: payload = random.choice(payloads) workflow = ( first_stage.s(payload) | group(group_task.s() for _ in range(NUM_GROUP_TASKS)) | last_stage.si() ) result = workflow.apply_async() for mapping in result.backend._pending_results: logger.info(f"Number of pending_results: {len(mapping)}") # Calling get seems to fix the leak # try: # result.get(timeout=0.1) # except celery.exceptions.TimeoutError: # ... result.forget() time.sleep(PACKET_DELAY) if __name__ == "__main__": main() ```

# Expected Behavior I expect to observe a steady memory usage. # Actual Behavior I'm testing an app that submits messages to the task queue from an MQTT broker. For some reason the memory usage of both the redis broker and the app keeps steadily increasing. On the redis side the number of messages in the queue is constant, while the client output buffers keep increasing in size. I used memray to analyze the app. Added 3 outputs from running the app progressively longer each time. It's also clear that the kombu connections are using more and more memory. Will continue to debug. Memray graphs: - https://gist.github.com/tsoos99dev/629ae7db4dbb0bf62228029ccc03b1aa - https://gist.github.com/tsoos99dev/7ceff0d0aa631df93b8a452f29d2e667 - https://gist.github.com/tsoos99dev/d36393154037e0a4cd12d97632efef01 Here's the live mode output after a few hours.

issue.title: Fix memory leak in exception handling (Issue #8882)
issue.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes a critical memory leak in Celery's exception handling that was causing significant memory growth when tasks raise unhandled exceptions.

## Problem

**Issue #8882** reported that Celery tasks raising unhandled exceptions were causing memory leaks:
- Memory not being garbage collected due to reference cycles
- Worse on Python 3.11+ due to enhanced traceback data

Closes #8882

This PR addresses a critical memory leak in Celery's exception handling by breaking reference cycles in tracebacks, ensuring frame locals are cleared, and adding comprehensive tests to verify the fix.

-     Add traceback_clear calls and explicit deletion of traceback references in retry, failure, and signal-handling paths

-     Enhance traceback_clear to efficiently clear frame data and update its docstring

-     Introduce unit and integration tests to validate that tracebacks no longer retain memory across various exception scenarios
